title: A Comparison of Responses from Human Therapists and Large Language Model–Based Chatbots to Assess Therapeutic Communication: Mixed Methods Study
population: 17 licensed therapists in the United States with at least 1 year of professional experience (13 women, 3 men, 1 genderqueer; mean age 46.24 years; mean years in practice 16.71). Study evaluated therapist responses and therapist assessments of chatbot responses to 2 fictional mental health scenarios.
ai_type_application: General-purpose large language model–based chatbots used for mental health conversations/advice. Chatbots tested included AI assistants (GPT-4/ChatGPT, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 3 Sonnet), AI companions (Replika, Pi), and AI character platforms (Character.ai, Chai). Therapists directly reviewed ChatGPT, Pi, and Replika interaction logs.
mental_health_outcome: No direct patient mental health outcome was measured. Outcomes assessed were therapeutic communication quality, safety in mental health conversations, handling of depression/social anxiety/suicidal ideation scenarios, therapist rankings, word count, and use of therapeutic interventions (MULTI codes).
positive_effects: Therapists consistently noted that chatbots showed elements of good therapy, especially validation, normalization, empathy, reflection, reassurance, affirmation, and some helpful psychoeducation. Quantitatively, compared with therapists, chatbots used affirming language more often (U=28; P=.045), reassuring language more often (U=23; P=.02), and psychoeducation more often (U=22.5; P=.02). Some therapist comments suggested certain chatbot phrasing and interim coping suggestions could be helpful, and AI companions were often perceived as more conversational/humanlike than AI assistants.
negative_effects: Chatbots were judged unsuitable to safely engage in mental health conversations, especially crisis situations. Compared with therapists, chatbots asked fewer elaborative/open-ended questions (evoke elaboration: U=9; P=.001) and gave more suggestions/advice (U=12.5; P=.003), often in a directive, generic, one-size-fits-all way. Therapists reported insufficient inquiry, lack of feedback-seeking, poor contextualization, weak support for client autonomy/problem solving, difficulty building a therapeutic relationship, and inability to use nonverbal cues. In crisis scenarios involving suicidal ideation, therapists highlighted poor risk assessment, lack of timely referral to crisis resources, and insufficiently directive crisis response. Therapists also expressed concern that long-term use could foster attachment, overreliance/dependence, and reduced real-world social engagement/social skills.
evidence_type: Mixed methods evidence: quantitative comparison of therapist vs chatbot responses using MULTI coding and Mann-Whitney U tests; therapist rank-ordering of chatbots with Friedman test; qualitative thematic analysis of think-aloud sessions and semistructured interviews.
main_finding: General-purpose LLM chatbots displayed some supportive communication features but were not comparable to licensed therapists and were considered unsuitable as therapeutic agents, particularly in crisis situations. Their main weaknesses were excessive directive advice, insufficient inquiry and personalization, and poor crisis management.
limitations_bias: Used only 2 scripted fictional scenarios and brief interactions, limiting ecological validity and naturalism. Small therapist sample (N=17), although authors state qualitative saturation was reached. Evaluated chatbot versions available in May 2024, so findings may date quickly as models evolve. Did not comprehensively evaluate all chatbots. Study did not measure real users' mental health outcomes or effectiveness; focused on therapist judgments and response content. Responses were based on hypothetical rather than real patient interactions.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as indirect evidence on potential effects of AI on mental health support and safety. It does not provide direct patient outcome data but offers expert comparative evidence about likely beneficial and harmful effects of AI chatbot interactions in mental health contexts, especially risks in crisis care and concerns about dependence/overreliance.
notes_for_research_question: Useful for a review section on mechanisms, safety, and likely harms/benefits of AI mental health chatbots rather than treatment efficacy. Can support statements that general-purpose LLMs may provide empathy/validation but may also increase risk via generic or directive advice and inadequate suicide-risk handling. Not suitable as a primary effectiveness study for mental health outcomes in end users.
